choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This leaves out the `V` printed by `this()`. `Vehicle(int)` begins with `this()`, which runs `Vehicle()` before the rest of its own body.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: `new Taxi()` calls `this(4)`, and `Taxi(int)` implicitly calls `super()`: `Car()` calls `Vehicle()`, which prints V; then C; then T4; then `Taxi()` prints T, giving VCT4T. `new Car(2)` calls `super(2)`, i.e. `Vehicle(int)`, which calls `this()` (V) and prints V2; then C2.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This assumes `Car(int)` runs only the no-argument `Vehicle()` constructor. `super(w)` runs `Vehicle(int)`, which calls `this()` and then prints V2.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This prints T before T4. `Taxi()` first calls `this(4)`, so `Taxi(int)` finishes (printing T4) before `Taxi()` prints its own T.

explanation: A constructor first runs another constructor (`this(...)` or `super(...)`, or an implicit `super()`), and only then its own statements, so output appears from the top of the hierarchy down.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This leaves out the `+ "!"` that `C.g()` appends after calling `super.g()`.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: `x` refers to a `C`. `x.f()` is `"C" + super.f()`, and `B.f()` is `super.f() + "B"`, which gives CAB. `x.g()` runs `C.g()`, which calls `A.g()` (B does not override `g`); inside it `f()` is `C`'s version, so it returns CABg, and `!` is added. For a `B`, `A.g()` calls `B.f()`, giving ABg.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This puts the `C` after the result of `super.f()`. `C.f()` returns `"C" + super.f()`, so the `C` comes first.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This assumes the call to `f()` inside `A.g()` runs `A`'s own version. The call is made on the actual object, so an overriding `f()` in `B` or `C` runs instead.

explanation: `super.method()` runs the superclass version on the same object, and any call to an overridden method made inside it still uses the object's actual class.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: `a` is declared as `Animal`, and the compiler can choose only among the methods of `Animal`, which has just `meet(Animal)`. `Dog`'s `meet(Dog)` cannot be reached through an `Animal` variable.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The overloaded method is chosen from the declared type of the argument: `a` is declared `Animal`, so `d.meet(a)` uses `meet(Animal)`, not `meet(Dog)`.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This ignores `Dog`'s version of `meet(Animal)`. It overrides the one in `Animal`, so it runs whenever the object is a `Dog`.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Which overload is used is decided at compile time from the declared types; which version of it runs is decided by the object. `a.meet(a2)` and `a.meet(d)`: only `meet(Animal)` is visible through `Animal`, and the object is a `Dog`, so D-A. `d.meet(a)`: the argument is declared `Animal`, so `meet(Animal)`, D-A. `d.meet(d)`: `meet(Dog)`, D-D. `a2.meet(d)`: A-A.

explanation: Overloading is resolved from the declared types at compile time; overriding is resolved from the actual object at run time.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This runs the superclass versions. `setup()` and `show()` are called on the object being constructed, which is a `Derived`, so the overriding versions run even though the calls are in `Base`'s constructor.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: `setup()` assigns 3 to `n` before `show()` is called, so `show()` prints n=3. The default value 0 applies only until `setup()` runs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: `new Derived()` runs `Base()` first. It calls `setup()` and `show()` on the new `Derived` object: `setup()` sets `n` to 3 and prints D-setup, and `show()` prints n=3. Only after `super()` returns does `Derived` run its field initializer (`n = 7`), and then its own constructor prints D7.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This assumes the initializer `n = 7` runs before the superclass constructor. It runs after `super()` returns, so it overwrites the 3 and `n` is 7 when `Derived` prints.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: While `Base`'s constructor runs, `Derived`'s field initializer has not run yet, and `setup()` has just set `n` to 3, so `show()` prints n=3.

explanation: Field initializers of a subclass run after the superclass constructor finishes, so an overridden method called from the superclass constructor sees the subclass's fields before they are initialized.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This leaves out the base pay: `Manager.pay()` returns `super.pay() + 100 * reports`.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This assumes the intern's `toString` prints only the name. It calls `super.toString()`, which adds a colon and the pay.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The pays are Ann 1000.0, Bo 2000 + 3 * 100 = 2300.0 and Cy 500 / 2 = 250.0, so the total is 3550.0. `Employee.toString()` calls `pay()` on the actual object, so Bo prints as Bo:2300.0. `Intern.toString()` adds `Intern ` to the front: Intern Cy:250.0.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This uses every employee's base pay (1000 + 2000 + 500). Each element of the list is a different kind of object, and `pay()` runs that object's own version.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: This leaves out the word Intern. `Intern` overrides `toString` and puts `Intern ` in front of `super.toString()`.

explanation: Through an `Employee` reference, each call to an overridden method runs the version belonging to the object's actual class, including a call made inside an inherited method such as `toString`.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This compiles and runs. A `Circle` is a `Shape`, so it can be stored in an array of `Shape`.

choices.label: B
choices.text: `Shape s = new Circle(); String n = s.name();`
choices.explanation: This compiles and runs. `name()` is declared in `Shape`, and at run time `Circle`'s version is used.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This compiles, because the cast from a superclass to a subclass is allowed at compile time. It throws a `ClassCastException` at run time, since the object is not a `Circle`, but that is not a compile-time error.

choices.label: D
choices.text: `Shape s = new Circle(); double r = s.radius();`
choices.explanation: The compiler checks method calls against the declared type. `s` is declared as `Shape`, which has no `radius()` method, so the call does not compile (a cast to `Circle` would be needed).

choices.label: E
choices.text: `Object o = new Circle(); String t = o.toString();`
choices.explanation: This compiles and runs. Every class inherits `toString()` from `Object`.

explanation: The compiler only allows calls to methods in the declared type of a variable; a downcast compiles but may fail at run time.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: `a` was created with `new Animal()`, so casting it to `Dog` throws a `ClassCastException` (y); an object can be cast only to its own class or to one of its superclasses.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Casting to `Animal` does not change the object. `b` still refers to a `Dog`, so `Dog`'s `sound()` runs and returns Woof.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: `b` refers to a `Dog`, so `(Dog) b` works (1). `a` refers to an `Animal`, which is not a `Dog`, so the second cast throws (y). A `Dog` is not a `Puppy`, so the third cast throws (z). The final upcast does not change the object, so `Dog.sound()` returns Woof.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This assumes `b` refers to a `Puppy`. It was created with `new Dog()`, so the cast to `Puppy` fails, and `Dog`'s `sound()` runs at the end.

explanation: A cast succeeds at run time only if the object is an instance of the target type (its own class or a subclass of it).

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The declared type does not decide which method runs. `c` refers to a `Skipper`, so `c.step()` returns 2.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: `c.inc()` runs `Skipper`'s `inc()`, which adds twice per call, and `step()` inside it is the `Skipper`'s version (2), so each call adds 4.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: `c.inc()` runs `Skipper.inc()`, which calls `Counter.inc()` twice. Each of those adds `step()` on the same object, so it is `Skipper`'s `step()`, 2. Each call adds 4, so after two calls `get()` is 8. `c.step()` also returns 2.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This ignores `Skipper`'s own `inc()`. The variable's declared type is `Counter`, but the object is a `Skipper`, so `Skipper.inc()` runs and calls `super.inc()` twice.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: Each call to `inc()` runs `super.inc()` twice, and each of those adds `step()`, which is 2 for a `Skipper`. Two calls add 8, not 2.

explanation: `super.inc()` runs the superclass code, but a call to `step()` inside it still uses the version of `step()` belonging to the object's actual class.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: `o.equals(a)` is called through an `Object` variable, which has only `equals(Object)`. That method compares references, and `b` and `a` are different objects: false.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This treats `equals(Point)` as an override of `equals(Object)`. A method with a different parameter type overloads it; calls whose argument is declared `Object` still use the inherited version.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: In `a.equals(o)`, `o` is declared as `Object`, so the compiler picks `equals(Object)` (inherited from `Object`), which compares references: false.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: `equals(Point)` overloads, rather than overrides, `Object.equals(Object)`. `a.equals(b)`: the argument is declared `Point`, so `equals(Point)` runs: true. In the other three calls the argument is declared `Object` or the call is made through an `Object` variable, so the inherited `equals(Object)` compares references, and `a` and `b` are different objects: false false false.

explanation: To override a method, the name and the parameter types must match exactly; otherwise it is an overload, chosen from the declared types.

choices.label: B

explanation: Every constructor in the chain runs, and a `static` counter in the superclass is shared by objects of all its subclasses.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Using `super.` does not give access to a `private` field. This causes a compile-time error.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: `Account` does not have a `setBalance` method, so this does not compile.

choices.explanation: `balance` is `private` in `Account`, so it cannot be accessed by name in the subclass. This causes a compile-time error.

explanation: A subclass inherits public methods but cannot use the superclass's private fields by name; it must go through the superclass's public methods.

explanation: If a subclass constructor does not call `super(...)` explicitly, the compiler inserts `super()`, so the superclass needs a no-argument constructor or the subclass must call one of its other constructors first.
